stories.title: From Idea to Enterprise: How One Founder Used AI to Launch a Mental Health Startup in Record Time
stories.summary: Michelle Turner, a former foster parent with no business background, used AI as a mentor to launch Here Now Health, a virtual behavioral-health company for kids in foster care. Founded in January 2025, it's already Medicaid-certified in three states and employs 16 people.
stories.extended_summary: Michelle Turner had cared for over 40 children as a foster parent and adopted four, but she had no MBA, no investors, and no formal business training. From her home office, she turned AI tools into her personal mentor—drafting her business plan, learning startup fundamentals, and refining pitches. In just months, she founded Here Now Health, a virtual behavioral-health company for children in the child welfare system. Now Medicaid-certified in three states with 16 employees, her startup is already counseling kids entering foster care.

stories.title: From Madonna's hairdresser to tech founder: Minista Jazz is keeping receipts on the age of AI
stories.summary: Minista Jazz, who spent decades as a touring hairstylist for Madonna and Miley Cyrus, became a tech founder at 45. After seeing her own image used online without consent, she built Much Different World, an AI-era consent registry that uses voice fingerprinting to protect digital identities.
stories.extended_summary: For years, Minista Jazz styled the hair of pop icons—Madonna, Miley Cyrus. But when she found her own image being used online without permission, she knew she had to act. After her father's death, she enrolled in a coding bootcamp at 45, graduated in February 2025, and launched Much Different World—a platform that lets people register their voices, likenesses, and creative work with cryptographic proof before AI can use it. Starting with voice registration, the system uses mathematical fingerprinting to verify human ownership, giving people a way to keep receipts in the age of AI.

stories.title: Student developer debuts a platform to help neurodivergent people find inclusive workplaces
stories.summary: Navya Tuteja, a 17-year-old in Northern Virginia, built Raaha, a free AI platform that helps neurodivergent people and those with invisible disabilities find inclusive jobs. Inspired by her hard-of-hearing mother, it scores job descriptions on seven fit factors and offers an interview-practice chatbot.
stories.extended_summary: At 17, Navya Tuteja built Raaha—a free AI platform that helps neurodivergent workers and people with invisible disabilities figure out if a job is really a good fit. She was inspired by watching her hard-of-hearing mother navigate workplace accommodations. Built on school nights and spring break using Claude's API and trained on real job postings, Raaha scores pasted job descriptions on seven fit factors. It also includes a chatbot for practicing accommodation request conversations. Since launching in June 2026, it already has 150 users.

stories.title: South Boston Boys & Girls Club teens build AI app designed to keep parents connected
stories.summary: Joshua Moreta, 13, and Gabriel Hinson, 15, led a team to build an AI-powered achievement tracker app for their South Boston Boys & Girls Club. The app lets parents see their child's progress and recommends new clubs, and the club plans to roll it out soon.
stories.extended_summary: Two teens from the South Boston Boys & Girls Club—Joshua Moreta, just 13, and Gabriel Hinson, 15—didn't just participate in an AWS hackathon; they led a team of four to build an app that keeps parents connected. Their AI-powered achievement tracker lets staff check off members' accomplishments while parents log in to see real-time progress. The app even recommends new clubs based on what a member already enjoys. The club's leadership is already planning to roll it out to staff, members, and families.
